messages.author: 1f723d378f24adbb
messages.subject: quick reference card / cheat sheet
parts:
Hi,

Is there a quick reference card / cheat sheet for stan? Ie something
that fits on 4-10 pages, contains the skeleton of a typical Stan file,
but is less formal than the BNF grammar in the manual, and the
distributions in some compact form (various functions [cdf/pdf/...] all
follow a common form, so this could be organized into a small
space). Something similar to http://clqr.boundp.org/ for Common Lisp, or
https://www.stat.auckland.ac.nz/~stat782/downloads/auctex.pdf for
AUCTeX.

Best,

Tamas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] quick reference card / cheat sheet
parts:
No, we don't have one, but I think it'd be very useful, so
I'm creating a feature request for the modeling language
and assigning it to myself:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/868

We could also use one for PyStan, CmdStan and RStan.

The downside is that with more doc, it's much harder to
keep in synch (takes more time, inconsistencies more likely).

- Bob

messages.author: b82af643aafe86d2
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] quick reference card / cheat sheet
parts:
Krzysztof Sakrejda <krzysztof...@gmail.com> writes:

> On Wednesday, August 13, 2014 1:38:21 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>> The downside is that with more doc, it's much harder to
>> keep in synch (takes more time, inconsistencies more likely).
>>
>
> I don't know how you make your docs (plain LaTeX?) but at least with knitr
> (which will mix LaTeX with R/Python and other languages) it's possible to
> include outside
> scripts as chunks of code. That might take care of inconsistencies.

Org-mode under Emacs does that, too.

I see in a separate note that you use LaTeX. One tool that might have
advantages is DocBook (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DocBook). It is
designed to make it easier to pull together pre-defined chunks that you
reuse in various documents -- "Write once, read anywhere."

For example, you write the chunks that you need for various documents,
and you assemble the pieces you need from those chunks for each document
you want. You can, at least to a significant degree, use the equivalent
of variables in text, so that you could have one document for generic
Stan and plug in CmdStan, RStan, PyStan, or any other Stan as
appropriate to the document you're generating.

Then you process the document to produce a PDF manual, an online Web
page, or whatever you need. I tend to use the route through dblatex to
create PDFs, so that turns the DocBook source into LaTeX on its way to
PDF.

As DocBook source is XML and XML can be wordy, you may want help in
creating it. I've used Emacs' nxml-mode and found it good. I'm told
there are GUI approaches (perhaps in LibreOffice).

DITA is a similar, alternative approach I've read about but never used.

Of course, perhaps LaTeX is exactly what you want.

Bill
